name: Lingala
notes: Lingala (lingála), Bantu lingua franca of the Congo river basin. Literary Lingala has a seven-vowel system /a e ɛ i o ɔ u/ written with the IPA letters ⟨ɛ ɔ⟩; spoken Lingala reduces this to five. Prenasalised sequences are written ⟨mb mp nd ng nk ns nt nz⟩ and ⟨gb⟩ is the labial-velar /ɡ͡b/. Lingala is tonal — the acute marks high tone, the circumflex falling and the caron rising — but tone is NOT emitted here: the accented vowels map to the same phoneme as their plain counterparts so that accented text still transcribes.

sources.author: Redden, James E.; Bongo, F.
sources.title: Lingala Basic Course (Foreign Service Institute Basic Course Series)
sources.publisher: Foreign Service Institute, U.S. Department of State (public domain; livelingua.com mirror)
sources.notes: The introduction's four-column chart (pp. xi-xiii: orthographic symbol, phoneme, phonetic realisation, English or French comparison), read in full. It gives ⟨p t k b d g f s h z m n ny l w y⟩ with ⟨z⟩ realised [z, dz, dʒ], the labial-velars ⟨kp gb ngb⟩ as simultaneous articulations, ⟨v r⟩ confined to unassimilated loans, and two contrastive tones. Its footnote 3 says the practical orthography does not separate the two mid vowels: written ⟨e⟩ is usually /e/ but sometimes /ɛ/, written ⟨o⟩ usually /o/ but sometimes /ɔ/, which is why this map's ⟨ɛ ɔ⟩ keys belong to the literary spelling and not to the everyday one. Note 4 (p. xiv) adds that ⟨kp gb ngb⟩ are very rare, usually explosive, and implosive for some speakers. Two gaps against the map: ⟨kp⟩ and ⟨ngb⟩ have no key here while ⟨gb⟩ does. A 1963 language course whose transcription is a Bloomfieldian phonemic one, not IPA, read for the letter-to-phoneme chart and the seven-versus-five vowel note; the OCR of this scan is poor and the chart was read on the page image.
